lines.text: Canal Street is carrying 12.2 cars per 100 m on a two‑lane segment and jams at level 7 during the 18:00 rush hour, contributing to the city‑wide 70% speed loss. Reducing peak‑hour demand by a third will immediately ease congestion without any demolition or new construction. I recommend we implement staggered office hours (Option C) as the most cost‑effective, low‑impact solution.

lines.text: I support the staggered office hours because cutting peak‑hour traffic by a third will directly reduce emissions from the 125 vehicles queuing, helping the 89 residents currently breathing polluted air. This low‑impact solution preserves existing green space and avoids demolition, matching our environmental priorities.

lines.text: I support the staggered office hours as it eases congestion without demolishing jobs or threatening our housing stock. lines.text: I continue to back the staggered office‑hour policy because it eases congestion without consuming land that could be zoned for housing or displacing any jobs. lines.text: I remain comfortable with option A; the $2,800 outlay reduces the treasury to $93,237 and the monthly balance to $1,385, preserving a healthy surplus while restoring water to the 298 affected residents.

lines.text: Mayor, Canal Street is at 12.2 cars per 100 m on a two‑lane segment and jams at level 7 during the 18:00 rush, costing drivers 70 % of normal speed city‑wide. I propose we construct the new parallel relief street (Option B) at a $960 upfront cost, which adds a two‑lane alternative without demolishing any jobs or homes. This will divert a significant share of traffic, easing the bottleneck while staying within the budget.
lines.condition: Provide proper connection points to existing network

lines.text: Mayor, from a welfare perspective the relief street avoids any displacement of homes or jobs and stays under the $1,500 upfront limit, which aligns with our mandate to protect residents. It should ease the rush‑hour jam, helping the 376 nearby residents who currently endure long delays, and the low monthly cost means we won’t have to raise taxes that would further strain the 28% unemployment rate.
lines.condition: Include noise mitigation measures for nearby residents

lines.text: Mayor, while a new relief street would add capacity, it risks inducing more traffic and offers little emission reduction. I recommend we implement staggered office hours (Option C) which cuts peak‑hour traffic by a third without any construction or loss of green space. This approach directly lowers vehicle emissions for the 125 cars on Canal Street and helps the 89 residents currently breathing polluted air. We should monitor compliance to ensure the intended traffic smoothing.
lines.condition: require ≥80% employer enrollment

lines.text: I support the relief street proposal as it eases the bottleneck without demolishing any homes or jobs, preserving the housing‑workplace balance that our department must protect. The low upfront cost respects the mayor's budget ceiling and avoids displacing the 376 nearby residents.
lines.condition: align the new street to avoid encroaching on earmarked housing plots

lines.text: Mayor, with the treasury at $96,037 and a projected monthly surplus of $1,495, the $960 upfront cost and $3 extra monthly spend of Option B leaves us well within our limits, preserving a healthy balance while staying under the $1,500 ceiling; it also avoids demolition costs, making it the most fiscally prudent choice.

Mayor, while the relief street stays within budget, it will likely induce additional traffic and offers no real emission cut; staggered office hours cut peak traffic by a third without new construction, directly lowering emissions for the 125 vehicles and helping the 89 residents breathing polluted air. I therefore oppose B and back C.

Mayor, the relief street still offers the most direct capacity increase without demolishing jobs, staying under the $1,500 cap and adding only $3 a month, which fits our budget. It will divert a sizable share of the 125 vehicles on Canal Street, cutting the jam level from 7 to a manageable flow and preserving emergency routes. To address the environmental concern, we will install noise barriers and monitor traffic volumes to prevent induced demand.
lines.condition: Include noise mitigation and traffic demand monitoring

lines.text: Mayor, from a housing perspective the relief street respects our mandate by avoiding any demolition of homes or workplaces and preserves the existing residential fabric, while still addressing the Canal Street bottleneck. lines.condition: align the new street to avoid earmarked housing plots

lines.text: Mayor, the relief street aligns with our mandate to protect the 376 residents nearby, avoids any displacement, and stays under the $1,500 upfront limit, helping to reduce rush‑hour stress without raising taxes that would burden the 28% unemployed. I continue to back Option B, provided we include noise mitigation measures for the adjoining neighbourhoods.
lines.condition: Include noise mitigation measures for nearby residents

lines.text: Mayor, the treasury sits at $96,037 with a projected $1,495 surplus; the $960 upfront and $3 monthly outlay of Option B leaves the balance essentially untouched, whereas Option C would chew $350 each month and shrink our cushion. Staying under the $1,500 ceiling and avoiding any demolition, the relief street gives the best value for money. I therefore continue to support Option B.

issue.title: Gridlock on Canal Street
facts: Canal Street (street, 1 lane each way, 96 m segment) in the city centre.
Traffic on it: 12.2 cars per 100 m; it jams at about 7. Time of day 18:00 (rush hour).
Across the city, queues cost drivers 70% of their normal speed.
Residents living within 200 m of this road: 376.
Nearest clinic to this road: none in the city. Nearest school: none in the city.
Nearest fire station: none in the city. Nearest police station: none in the city.

options.title: Widen Canal Street to a four-lane avenue
facts: Rebuilds this 96 m segment with two lanes each way and a median: roughly double the capacity, and more traffic drawn onto it.
The wider road takes the front of neighbouring lots: demolishes 40 homes (1,380 residents) and 6 workplaces (210 jobs).
Nearest clinic to Canal Street: none in the city. Nearest school: none in the city.

options.title: New relief street parallel to Canal Street
facts: A 96 m two-lane street about 56 m to the west of Canal Street, joining the network at 2 points, so drivers get a second route.
It runs over open land: no buildings demolished.
Nearest clinic to the new street: none in the city. Nearest school: none in the city.
Clears almost no trees.

options.title: Staggered office hours (policy)
facts: The city pays employers $350 a month to spread start and finish times.
Traffic at the height of the morning and evening rush drops by about a third, spread over a longer period; the number of trips stays the same.
Nothing is built or demolished. It can be dropped later.

options.title: Take no action for now
facts: Nothing is built or changed. The problem is likely to continue.

lines.text: Mayor, Canal Street is operating at 12.2 cars per 100 m and jams at 7 pm, which is unsustainable. I propose we build the new parallel relief street (Option B) because it adds a second two‑lane corridor without displacing residents or jobs and costs only $960 upfront plus $3 a month. It will divert enough traffic to bring speeds back toward normal while keeping our emergency routes clear.
lines.condition: ensure signal coordination at junctions

lines.text: Mayor, the data show Canal Street is at 12.2 cars per 100 m and jams at 7 pm, so we need capacity relief without displacing residents. The parallel relief street (Option B) adds a two‑lane alternative at minimal cost and no demolition, which will divert enough traffic to restore speeds. I maintain my support for Option B, provided we synchronize signals at the intersecting junctions.
lines.condition: ensure signal coordination at junctions
